concepts.title: Figure & Subplots Setup
concepts.intro: plt.figure() controls canvas. plt.subplots() creates Figure+Axes in one call. Most common entry point for all matplotlib workflows.
concepts.explanation: In matplotlib the `Figure` is the whole canvas and each `Axes` is one plot panel — every chart you build starts by deciding how many panels you need and how they are arranged. `plt.figure()` creates a bare canvas you bolt panels onto later, but the workhorse is `plt.subplots(nrows, ncols)`: it returns a `(fig, axes)` pair in a single call. With both `nrows` and `ncols` greater than 1, `axes` is a 2D array and `axes.flat` walks it in row-major (reading) order — top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right — which is also the order of `fig.axes`. For one-row or one-column layouts you get a 1D array (pass `squeeze=False` if you always want 2D). Two figure-level arguments matter everywhere: `figsize=(width, height)` sizes the canvas in inches, and `fig.suptitle()` stamps one title across all panels (`fig.get_suptitle()` reads it back). Layout helpers go further: `sharex=True` / `sharey=True` chain panels so zooming one rescales its partner — ideal for paired time series — and `gridspec_kw` (`width_ratios`, `height_ratios`) skews cell sizes without abandoning the grid. The classic beginner traps: unpacking a 2D axes array as if it were flat (`fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2)` crashes), forgetting `figsize` is (width, height) not (height, width), and mixing up `plt.subplot` (singular, one panel) with `plt.subplots` (the grid factory). The two exercises ahead drill exactly this: a 2x2 sensor wall titled in reading order, then a twin launch report whose two panels must genuinely share one x-axis.
keyPoints: `plt.subplots(nrows, ncols)` returns `(fig, axes)`; with a 2D grid, `axes` is a 2D array and `fig.axes` lists the panels in row-major creation order.
`axes.flat` iterates any-shape axes array in reading order (top-left to bottom-right).
`sharex=True` / `sharey=True` link axes: `set_xlim` on one panel moves every partner panel.
`figsize=(width, height)` is in inches; `fig.get_size_inches()` returns it as an array.
`fig.suptitle()` sets a figure-wide title above all panels; `fig.get_suptitle()` reads it back.
`squeeze=False` forces a 2D axes array even for 1xN or Nx1 grids.

blocks.title: figure() / subplots() — all params
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# plt.figure() — main params
fig = plt.figure(
    num=1,             # id — reuse if already exists
    figsize=(10,6),    # (width,height) inches. 10,6 = medium
    dpi=100,           # dots per inch
    facecolor="white",
    layout="tight",    # "tight" "constrained" None
)
plt.close()

# plt.subplots — the standard way
fig, ax    = plt.subplots()                  # single ax
fig, axes  = plt.subplots(2,3,figsize=(12,8))# 2x3 grid → (2,3) ndarray
fig,(a1,a2)= plt.subplots(1,2,sharex=True)  # share x axis

# squeeze=False ensures axes is always 2D
fig, axes  = plt.subplots(1,3,squeeze=False) # shape (1,3)

# Width/height ratios via gridspec_kw
fig, axes  = plt.subplots(1,2,
    gridspec_kw={"width_ratios":[3,1],"wspace":0.1},
    figsize=(10,4))

# figsize quick reference:
# (4,3) tiny  (6,4) small  (10,6) medium
# (12,8) large  (16,9) widescreen  (20,14) poster
print("figsize and subplots documented")
plt.close("all")

concepts.title: All Plot Types
concepts.intro: 18 distinct plot types. Each has unique parameters. The fmt shorthand for plot() is '[color][marker][linestyle]' e.g. 'r--o'.
concepts.explanation: Every matplotlib chart is a call that hangs *artists* off an `Axes`, and knowing which container each plot type fills is half the battle. `ax.plot()` appends `Line2D` objects to `ax.lines`; `ax.bar()` and `ax.barh()` drop `Rectangle` patches into `ax.patches` — bar heights read back with `get_height()`, horizontal-bar lengths with `get_width()`. `ax.hist()` also fills `ax.patches`, one rectangle per bin, and each patch's `get_height()` is the count — remember that `bins=[edges]` produces `len(edges) - 1` bars and that the final bin closes on the right, so the boundary value lands in the last bin. `ax.scatter()` and `ax.fill_between()` create collections instead: a scatter's points live in `ax.collections[i].get_offsets()` as an `(N, 2)` array you can read back point-for-point, and each extra `scatter` call is another collection. Line styling has a shorthand — the fmt string `'r--o'` parses as `[color][marker][linestyle]` — but explicit `color=`, `marker=`, `linestyle=` kwargs say the same thing more legibly. Two gotchas burn everyone: categorical x (passing strings straight to `bar`) gets tick labels for free, while plotting over numeric positions needs `set_xticks` + `set_xticklabels`; and artists land in their containers in *call order*, so `ax.lines[0]` is whichever series you plotted first. The exercises make you build a two-flock scatter map and a four-type telemetry board whose every panel is inspected programmatically.
keyPoints: `ax.plot()` appends `Line2D` to `ax.lines`; `ax.bar`/`ax.barh`/`ax.hist` fill `ax.patches`; `ax.scatter`/`ax.fill_between` add to `ax.collections`.
Bar patch heights come back via `get_height()` in call order; `barh` patch lengths via `get_width()`.
`hist(bins=[e0, e1, ...])` draws `len(edges) - 1` bars; the last bin is closed on the right, so the top edge value counts in it.
Scatter points are read back from `ax.collections[i].get_offsets()` — an `(N, 2)` array in input order; one collection per `scatter` call.
The `plot` fmt string is `[color][marker][linestyle]` (e.g. `'r--o'`); explicit `color=`/`marker=`/`linestyle=` kwargs are equivalent.
Artists join their containers in call order — the first series you draw is `ax.lines[0]`.

blocks.title: plot / scatter / bar / hist / boxplot / violin / pie / imshow / errorbar / fill_between
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, numpy as np

x=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,50)
fig,axes=plt.subplots(3,3,figsize=(12,10))

# 1. Line plot
axes[0,0].plot(x,np.sin(x),color="C0",lw=2,ls="--",marker="o",ms=3,label="sin")
axes[0,0].plot(x,np.cos(x),"r-.",lw=1.5,label="cos")
axes[0,0].set_title("plot()")

# 2. Scatter
np.random.seed(0)
xr,yr=np.random.randn(80),np.random.randn(80)
axes[0,1].scatter(xr,yr,s=30+50*np.abs(xr),c=yr,cmap="plasma",alpha=0.7)
axes[0,1].set_title("scatter()")

# 3. Bar
cats=["A","B","C","D"]; v=[23,45,12,67]
axes[0,2].bar(cats,v,width=0.6,color=["#FF6B6B","#4EC","#45B","#96C"],edgecolor="k")
axes[0,2].set_title("bar()")

# 4. Histogram
axes[1,0].hist(np.random.randn(500),bins=25,density=True,
    histtype="stepfilled",color="steelblue",alpha=0.8,edgecolor="white")
axes[1,0].set_title("hist()")

# 5. Boxplot
axes[1,1].boxplot([np.random.randn(50)*s for s in [1,2,0.5]],
    patch_artist=True,notch=True,labels=["narrow","wide","tight"])
axes[1,1].set_title("boxplot()")

# 6. Pie
axes[1,2].pie([35,30,20,15],labels=["Py","JS","Java","Other"],
    autopct="%1.0f%%",explode=[0.05,0,0,0],startangle=90)
axes[1,2].set_title("pie()")

# 7. imshow
axes[2,0].imshow(np.random.rand(8,8),cmap="viridis",aspect="auto")
axes[2,0].set_title("imshow()")

# 8. errorbar
xe=np.arange(5); ye=np.random.rand(5)*10
axes[2,1].errorbar(xe,ye,yerr=0.5+np.random.rand(5),fmt="o-",capsize=4,ecolor="red")
axes[2,1].set_title("errorbar()")

# 9. fill_between
xe2=np.linspace(0,4,50); ye2=np.sin(xe2)
axes[2,2].fill_between(xe2,ye2-0.3,ye2+0.3,alpha=0.3)
axes[2,2].plot(xe2,ye2)
axes[2,2].set_title("fill_between()")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_gallery.png",dpi=80)
print("8 plot types saved")
plt.close()

Every panel uses a different plot call, and the debrief script must assemble the board in the same slot order every weekend so nobody misreads a chart.
exercises.task:
Implement `solve(speeds, drivers, points, heart_rates, exercises, minutes)`: build `fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10))` and fill the panels in this exact slot order:

1. **Top-left** (`axes` index 0): line plot of `speeds` against lap numbers `1..len(speeds)` with `marker='o'` and `linestyle='-'`; title `'Lap Speed'`.
2. **Top-right** (index 1): bar chart of `points` per driver with the driver names from `drivers` readable as x tick labels; title `'Points by Driver'`.
3. **Bottom-left** (index 2): histogram of `heart_rates` with `bins=[110, 120, 130, 140, 150]`; title `'Heart Rate Zones'`.
4. **Bottom-right** (index 3): horizontal bar chart of `minutes` per exercise from `exercises`; title `'Training Load'`.

Return the `Figure` object.
constraints: panel slot order is fixed: 0 line, 1 bar, 2 hist, 3 barh
heart rates all fall within [110, 150]
the histogram must use exactly the five bin edges given

concepts.title: Axes Customization
concepts.intro: Full control over every visual property: title, labels, ticks, legend, grid, spines, scale, and aspect ratio.
concepts.explanation: A raw plot answers *what the data looks like*; a customized axes answers *what it means*. The customization pass is a handful of setter calls on the `Axes` object. `ax.set_title`, `ax.set_xlabel` and `ax.set_ylabel` carry the narration. `ax.set_xticks([...])` pins tick *positions*; `ax.set_xticklabels([...])` renames them — call them in that order, because the new strings attach to whatever ticks currently exist. `ax.set_xlim` / `ax.set_ylim` freeze the viewport, and `get_xlim` / `get_ylim` report back exactly what you set. `ax.legend()` collects every artist that carries a `label=` kwarg — which is why `plot(..., label='p95')` exists — and `get_legend().get_texts()` lists the entries it built. `ax.grid(True)` turns on gridlines, and `ax.set_yscale('log')` switches the y axis to logarithmic, mandatory when values span orders of magnitude and only sane for positive data. Read-backs make all of this verifiable: `get_yscale()` returns `'log'`, `get_xticklabels()` yields the current label strings, and the gridlines exposed by `get_xgridlines()` become visible. The traps: calling `set_xticklabels` without fixing ticks first (labels drift whenever the tick count changes), passing `labels=` to `plot` (the kwarg is `label=`), and assuming defaults where the grader asserts what the task explicitly set. Next up: a board-deck relabeling job, then a latency chart that only reads correctly on a log axis with pinned limits and both percentiles named in its legend.
keyPoints: `ax.set_xticks(positions)` fixes where ticks sit; `ax.set_xticklabels(labels)` renames them — set ticks first, then labels.
`ax.legend()` shows every artist carrying a `label=` kwarg; entries come back via `ax.get_legend().get_texts()`.
`ax.set_yscale('log')` rescales the y axis; `ax.get_yscale()` then returns `'log'`.
`ax.grid(True)` makes the gridlines in `ax.get_xgridlines()` / `get_ygridlines()` visible.
`set_xlim` / `set_ylim` pin the viewport; `get_xlim` / `get_ylim` return exactly the pinned values.
The plot kwarg is `label=` (singular) — `labels=` belongs to `set_xticklabels`.

blocks.title: set_title / xlabel / ylabel / ticks / tick_params / legend / grid / spines
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,5))
ax.plot([1,2,3,4],[1,4,9,16],"b-o",label="y=x²")
ax.plot([1,2,3,4],[1,2,3,4],"r--",label="y=x")

# Title & labels
ax.set_title("Custom Axes",fontsize=16,fontweight="bold",loc="center",pad=12)
ax.set_xlabel("Input",fontsize=13,labelpad=8)
ax.set_ylabel("Output",fontsize=13,labelpad=8)

# Limits
ax.set_xlim(0.5,4.5); ax.set_ylim(-1,18)

# Ticks
ax.set_xticks([1,2,3,4])
ax.set_xticklabels(["one","two","three","four"],rotation=20,ha="right")
ax.set_yticks(range(0,18,3))
ax.tick_params(axis="both",which="major",direction="out",
    length=6,width=1.2,color="gray",labelsize=11)
ax.minorticks_on()
ax.tick_params(axis="x",which="minor",length=3,width=0.8)

# Legend — all loc strings:
# 0=best 1=upper right 2=upper left 3=lower left 4=lower right
# 5=right 6=center left 7=center right 8=lower center
# 9=upper center 10=center
ax.legend(loc="upper left",fontsize=11,title="Legend",frameon=True,
    facecolor="#f8f8f8",edgecolor="gray",ncols=1,markerscale=1.2)

# Grid
ax.grid(True,which="major",axis="both",color="lightgray",ls="--",lw=0.7,alpha=0.8)

# Spines
ax.spines[["top","right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_linewidth(1.5)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color("#444")

# Scale options
ax.set_xscale("linear")   # "linear" "log" "symlog" "logit"

print("Axes customized")
plt.close()

exercises.title: Quarter Labels Makeover
exercises.story: The analyst's chart keeps going to the board deck with x ticks reading `0.0 1.0 2.0 3.0`, and the CFO has started returning it. The fix is pure axes customization: map tick positions to quarter names and dress the chart with a title, axis labels, and a legend.
exercises.task: Implement `solve(quarters, sales)`: build a single-axes figure (`fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))`). Plot `sales` against positions `range(len(quarters))` with `marker='o'` and `label='sales'`. Set the title to `'Quarterly Sales'`, the x-axis label to `'Quarter'`, and the y-axis label to `'Revenue ($M)'`. Replace the numeric ticks with quarter names: call `ax.set_xticks(range(len(quarters)))` followed by `ax.set_xticklabels(quarters)`. Show a legend. Return the `Figure` object.

concepts.title: Annotations, Text & Reference Lines
concepts.intro: ax.annotate() adds arrows with text. ax.text() places text anywhere. axhline/axvline/axhspan/axvspan add reference markers.
concepts.explanation: A finished analysis chart usually needs three things the data itself cannot supply: free text, pointers, and reference lines. `ax.text(x, y, s)` drops a string at data coordinates. `ax.annotate(s, xy=..., xytext=..., arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->'))` draws an arrow whose tip sits at `xy` with the label at `xytext` — both default to data coordinates. Every string you place, by either call, lands in `ax.texts`, and an `Annotation` remembers its tip as the `.xy` attribute. Reference lines are the sneaky part: `ax.axhline(y)` and `ax.axvline(x)` look like decorations but are ordinary `Line2D` objects appended to `ax.lines` — so after one `axhline`, `ax.lines[1]` is that reference line, its `get_ydata()` returns `[y, y]`, and an `axvline`'s `get_xdata()` returns `[x, x]`. They appear in *call order*, which is why plotting your data series first keeps it at index 0. `ax.fill_between(x, y1, y2)` shades the band between two curves and adds a `PolyCollection` to `ax.collections`. The gotchas: `annotate`'s `xytext` is optional (without it the text sits at the tip); `axhline(0.5)` takes a *level*, not two endpoints; and an annotation added conditionally may legitimately be absent — an empty `ax.texts` can be the correct output for quiet data. The exercises ahead build a training log whose mean line, record marker, and best-week note are all computed from the data, then an SLA report whose breach annotation only exists when a reading actually crosses the limit.
keyPoints: `ax.annotate(text, xy=..., xytext=..., arrowprops=...)` adds an `Annotation` to `ax.texts`; its `.xy` attribute is the arrow tip.
`ax.text(x, y, s)` also lands in `ax.texts` — `[t.get_text() for t in ax.texts]` lists every string on the axes.
`ax.axhline(y)` / `ax.axvline(x)` are `Line2D` objects in `ax.lines`: `get_ydata()` gives `[y, y]`, `get_xdata()` gives `[x, x]`.
Artists join `ax.lines` in call order — plot the data series first so it stays at index 0.
`ax.fill_between(x, y1, y2)` adds one `PolyCollection` to `ax.collections`.
A conditional annotation may be absent: an empty `ax.texts` is a legitimate result when the condition never fires.

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, numpy as np

fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,5))
x=np.linspace(0,10,100)
ax.plot(x,np.sin(x)*np.exp(-0.1*x))

# annotate() — arrow + text
ax.annotate("peak",
    xy=(1.57,0.92),              # tip of arrow (data coords)
    xytext=(3.0,0.9),            # text position
    xycoords="data",
    textcoords="data",
    fontsize=12,color="red",
    arrowprops=dict(
        arrowstyle="->",          # "-" "->" "-|>" "simple" "fancy"
        color="red",lw=1.5,
        connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.2",
    ),
    ha="left",va="center",
)

# ax.text() — arbitrary text
ax.text(0.98,0.02,"note",         # x,y in axes coords
    transform=ax.transAxes,        # use axes fraction [0,1]
    ha="right",va="bottom",
    fontsize=9,color="gray",
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round",facecolor="linen",alpha=0.8),
)

# Reference lines (infinite)
ax.axhline(y=0,  color="black",lw=0.8,ls="-",zorder=0)
ax.axhline(y=0.5,color="green",lw=1.0,ls="--",label="y=0.5")
ax.axvline(x=np.pi,color="blue",ls=":",lw=1.2,label="x=π")

# Spans (shaded regions)
ax.axhspan(-0.2,0.2,alpha=0.1,color="yellow",label="zero band")
ax.axvspan(6,8,alpha=0.1,color="red",label="decay region")

ax.legend(loc="upper right",fontsize=9)
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_annotate.png",dpi=80,bbox_inches="tight")

concepts.title: Colors, Layout, Saving & 3D
concepts.intro: All color formats, colormap categories, savefig options, GridSpec layout, 3D surfaces, and rcParams for global style configuration.
concepts.explanation: Color in matplotlib is a small language: named colors (`'red'`), hex strings (`'#FF8C00'`), RGB/RGBA tuples, cycle refs (`'C0'`), and qualified names (`'tab:blue'`). When you pass a string to `plot(color=...)`, `line.get_color()` hands that same string back — which makes explicit brand palettes trivially checkable. Backgrounds behave differently: `ax.set_facecolor('lightgray')` *normalizes* the spec, so `ax.get_facecolor()` always returns an RGBA tuple like `(0.827, 0.827, 0.827, 1.0)` — compare tuples, not strings. Beyond single panels, `fig.add_gridspec(rows, cols)` carves the canvas into a grid whose cells can be sliced — `gs[:, 0]` spans a whole column — and handed to `fig.add_subplot(...)`; `fig.axes` then counts panels in creation order. Append `projection='3d'` to the same call and the slot becomes an `Axes3D` (`ax.name == '3d'`), where `ax.plot(x, y, z)` draws a 3D line whose data you read back with `line.get_data_3d()`. Colormaps color *mappable* artists (`scatter(c=...)`, `imshow`) and pair with `plt.colorbar(mappable, ax=ax, ...)`, and `fig.savefig()` exports to png/pdf/svg — but saving has no place in graded exercises (no filesystem), so layout and color do the work here. The traps: `get_color` echoes strings while `get_facecolor` normalizes to RGBA; a GridSpec slice and the axes it spawns are different objects; and 3D requires the `projection` kwarg at creation time, not after. Two exercises ahead: a brand-palette face-off, then a reentry console mixing a column-spanning 3D panel with 2D telemetry.
keyPoints: Color specs: names (`'red'`), hex (`'#FF8C00'`), RGB tuples, cycle refs (`'C0'`) — `line.get_color()` returns exactly the string you passed.
`ax.set_facecolor('lightgray')` normalizes: `ax.get_facecolor()` returns an RGBA tuple `(0.827, 0.827, 0.827, 1.0)`, not the name.
`fig.add_gridspec(rows, cols)` + `fig.add_subplot(gs[slice])` builds panels that span cells; `fig.axes` counts them in creation order.
`fig.add_subplot(projection='3d')` returns an `Axes3D` — identifiable by `ax.name == '3d'`.
A 3D line comes from `ax.plot(x, y, z)`; its data is read back with `line.get_data_3d()`.
`savefig()` (formats png/pdf/svg, `bbox_inches='tight'`, `dpi`) is for exporting files — never tested in the grader.

blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.cm as cm
import numpy as np

# ── Colors ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Named:   "red"  "steelblue"  "darkviolet"  "coral"
# Hex:     "#FF5733"  "#2196F3"
# RGB:     (0.2, 0.6, 0.8)
# RGBA:    (0.2, 0.6, 0.8, 0.5)
# CN:      "C0" "C1" ... "C9"   (default color cycle)
# Tableau: "tab:blue" "tab:orange" "tab:green" "tab:red"
# xkcd:   "xkcd:sky blue"
# Gray:   "0.5"  (string 0=black 1=white)

# ── Colormaps by category ───────────────────────────────────────────
# Sequential:   viridis plasma inferno magma Blues Greens Reds Purples
# Diverging:    RdBu coolwarm seismic PiYG
# Cyclic:       twilight hsv
# Qualitative:  tab10 tab20 Set1 Set2 Pastel1 Dark2 Accent
# Append _r to reverse any colormap: "viridis_r"

fig,ax=plt.subplots()
img=ax.imshow(np.random.rand(10,10),cmap="viridis",vmin=0,vmax=1)
cb = plt.colorbar(img,ax=ax,
    shrink=0.8,      # fraction of axes height
    aspect=20,       # ratio height:width
    pad=0.02,        # gap between plot and colorbar
    label="Value",
    ticks=[0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0],
    format="%.2f",
    orientation="vertical",  # "horizontal"
    extend="neither",  # "both" "min" "max" "neither"
)
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_colorbar.png",dpi=80,bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close()

# ── savefig — all params ────────────────────────────────────────────
# fig.savefig(fname, dpi, facecolor, format, bbox_inches, pad_inches, transparent, metadata)
# formats: "png" "pdf" "svg" "eps" "jpeg" "webp" "tiff"
# bbox_inches="tight" removes extra whitespace automatically
# transparent=True  — PNG with alpha channel

# ── GridSpec ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from matplotlib.gridspec import GridSpec
fig2=plt.figure(figsize=(10,7))
gs=GridSpec(3,3,figure=fig2,
    hspace=0.4,wspace=0.3,
    width_ratios=[2,1,1],height_ratios=[1,2,1])
ax_main=fig2.add_subplot(gs[0:2,0:2])
ax_tr  =fig2.add_subplot(gs[0,2])
ax_br  =fig2.add_subplot(gs[1,2])
ax_bot =fig2.add_subplot(gs[2,:])
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_gridspec.png",dpi=60,bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close()

# ── subplot_mosaic ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig3,axd=plt.subplot_mosaic("AB;CC",figsize=(8,6))
# axd is dict: {"A":ax, "B":ax, "C":ax}
axd["A"].set_title("A — narrow top")
axd["B"].set_title("B — narrow top")
axd["C"].set_title("C — full width")
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_mosaic.png",dpi=60,bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close()

# ── 3D plotting ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig4=plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))
ax3=fig4.add_subplot(111,projection="3d")
u,v=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,50),np.linspace(0,np.pi,50)
U,V=np.meshgrid(u,v)
X=np.cos(U)*np.sin(V); Y=np.sin(U)*np.sin(V); Z=np.cos(V)
ax3.plot_surface(X,Y,Z,cmap="coolwarm",alpha=0.85,
    linewidth=0,antialiased=True)
ax3.set_xlabel("X"); ax3.set_ylabel("Y"); ax3.set_zlabel("Z")
ax3.set_title("3D Sphere")
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_3d.png",dpi=80,bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close()

# ── rcParams ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import matplotlib as mpl
mpl.rcParams["figure.figsize"]  = (8,5)
mpl.rcParams["figure.dpi"]     = 100
mpl.rcParams["font.size"]      = 12
mpl.rcParams["font.family"]    = "DejaVu Sans"
mpl.rcParams["lines.linewidth"]= 2.0
mpl.rcParams["axes.labelsize"] = 13
mpl.rcParams["axes.titlesize"] = 15
mpl.rcParams["axes.grid"]      = True
mpl.rcParams["xtick.labelsize"]= 11
mpl.rcParams["legend.fontsize"]= 11
mpl.rcParams["savefig.dpi"]    = 150
mpl.rcParams["savefig.bbox"]   = "tight"
mpl.rcdefaults()               # reset all to defaults

print("Colors / layout / 3D / rcParams documented")
